Twenty Sixth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2008
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 24, pp 305-312
Glaciological Observations during 26 th Indian
Antarctic Expedition
Prakash K. Shrivastava, A. Dharwadkar, A. K. Nath and Jayapaul D.
Antarctica Division, Geological Survey of India, Faridabad
ABSTRACT
Dakshin Gangotri Glacier was identified in Schirmacher Range in 1983 by
the Second Indian Antarctic Expedition. Since then, its snout is being monitored
every year. It was observed that the snout is persistently receding at an average
rate of 65 to 70 cm per annum.  In 2007 again the snout showed the similar trend
of retreat. Observations spanning over two decades on the Ice shelf close to
Indian research base “Maitri” in central Dronning Maud Land reveal that the
snow accumulation has a strong temporal as well as spatial variability. Strong
wind events can greatly decrease the mass through snowdrift and/or sublimation,
especially during summer. The spatial variability of snow accumulation at the
km scale is one order of magnitude higher than temporal variability at the
decadal/secular scale. The sum total effect of temporal variability over two
decades has revealed a rhythmic pattern in the intensity of snow accumulation
which to a limited extent can be used for making short-term weather predictions.
INTRODUCTION
 A continuous glaciological programme, which was initiated by
GSI from the very first Indian Antarctic Expedition, resulted in collecting
valuable data and publications of scientific papers. During the 26th
Indian Antarctic Expedition, the glaciological works completed by GSI,
mainly include monitoring the snout of Dakshin Gangotri (DG) glacier
along with its western extension, snow accumulation and ablation on the
shelf area near India Bay region and ice core drilling (along with
NCAOR) on ice-shelf in India Bay region.

II) Snow accumulation or ablation study: The accumulation/ablation
of snow on the ice shelf in India bay region is being continuously
monitored by the GSI team since long time. This is being done by
measuring exposed heights of sixteen wooden stakes, placed
regularly at an interval of 50 m in square-grid pattern.  The net
snow accumulation on the Ice shelf area, in the India Bay region,
has increased with respect to the previous year (2006). Almost at
all observation stakes, snow has accumulated by 65 cm in thickness.
The accumulation/ablation data is shown in Table 3. The
accumulation and ablation studies in the last decade showed
influence of temporal and spatial factors. Maximum snow
accumulation takes place in the summer season while during winter
season the snow precipitation is the least (Beg et al., 1997 and
